Decisions

Should you trust your gut?

Intuition works well where you have lots of practice and quick feedback. Outside those areas, it misleads.

"Listen to your gut," some say. "Don't be swayed by first impressions," say others. Both can be true, depending on the situation.

A debate that ended in agreement

Daniel Kahneman, a Nobel laureate for his studies of thinking biases, was wary of intuition. Gary Klein studied firefighters, nurses and soldiers who made highly accurate intuitive decisions in seconds. In 2009 they wrote an article together to see what they agreed on.

Their conclusion: intuition is reliable when two conditions are met:

  • The environment has regularities that can be learnt: it is not pure chance.
  • The person has had a lot of practice with quick, clear feedback on whether they were right.

A veteran firefighter, a chess player or an emergency nurse meet those conditions. Someone trying to second-guess the stock market, predict politics or judge a person in a five-minute interview does not. And the danger is that the feeling of certainty is just as strong in both cases.

First impressions

Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal showed strangers silent video clips of university lecturers lasting only a few seconds. Their ratings matched fairly closely those given by students at the end of the course. We form very quick impressions that are sometimes accurate about traits such as warmth or enthusiasm. But they are also swayed by physical attractiveness or stereotypes, so it is best to treat them as hypotheses, not certainties.

Why free-form interviews fail

When hiring someone, many people trust their "gut" during an unstructured conversation. A major review by Frank Schmidt and John Hunter of eighty years of research found that structured interviews, with the same questions for all candidates and criteria set in advance, predict job performance better than unscripted interviews. Structuring the decision does not cancel intuition: it puts it to the test.

What usually helps

  • Ask yourself whether you have real experience in that area, with feedback on your hits and misses.
  • Be wary of intuition in new, rare decisions or where chance plays a big part.
  • Treat intuition as a signal, not a verdict: if something "doesn't add up", look into why.
  • Use written criteria for important decisions, such as hiring someone or buying a house.

References

  1. Kahneman, D. y Klein, G. (2009). Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree. American Psychologist, 64(6), 515–526.
  2. Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, fast and slow. Nueva York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux. (Trad. esp.: Pensar rápido, pensar despacio, Debate, 2012).
  3. Ambady, N. y Rosenthal, R. (1993). Half a minute: predicting teacher evaluations from thin slices of nonverbal behavior and physical attractiveness. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(3), 431–441.
  4. Schmidt, F. L. y Hunter, J. E. (1998). The validity and utility of selection methods in personnel psychology. Psychological Bulletin, 124(2), 262–274.
